Oblong Face Shape

By AI Rate Face · Updated September 8, 2026 · Reference choices

An oblong — sometimes called rectangular — contour is noticeably longer than it is wide, with forehead, cheek and jaw widths that stay relatively even down the face. Where an oval tapers, an oblong runs closer to parallel, and the extra length is the defining feature.

Check your own shape free →

The longest of the seven profiles, with widths that stay fairly even from forehead to jaw.

How to tell if your face is oblong

These visual cues can be checked in a mirror. If several do not fit, compare the neighbouring profiles below.

  • 01

    Face length is markedly greater than cheek width — around 1.6× or more.

  • 02

    The sides of the face run closer to parallel than they taper.

  • 03

    The forehead often reads as tall as well as the face being long.

  • 04

    The chin may be rounded or squared; length is what identifies the profile, not the chin.

What the detector matches you against

These are the exact reference values the oblong profile uses. Your photo is scored against all seven profiles on these five measurements, and the closest ones are returned as percentages rather than a single label.

MeasurementOblong referenceWhat it means
Face length / cheek width1.64Visible upper-face landmark to chin, divided by cheek-level landmark width; the model does not detect the exact hairline.
Forehead / cheek width0.84Temple-level width as a share of cheek width.
Jaw / cheek width0.80Jaw-corner width as a share of cheek width.
Jaw corner angle144°Higher is a softer, more curved corner; lower is a squarer one.
Chin taper angle100°Higher is a broader chin; lower is a more pointed one.

These reference values are hand-set design choices, not population averages fitted to a labelled dataset. They define what this tool means by oblong; another calculator using different landmarks will place the boundaries elsewhere.

If oblong does not feel right

Oval

The same taper, less length. Below roughly 1.5× length-to-width, the oval profile fits better.

Read the oval guide →

Square

Both keep even widths down the face. Square is short, oblong is long — the ratio decides it.

Read the square guide →

What tends to suit a oblong face

These are visual-balance conventions, not rules. They describe where volume, width or a line is usually placed to work with or against the natural contour — and either direction is a valid choice.

Hairstyles

  • •Add width with waves, curls or layers near the cheek area.
  • •A fringe can visually shorten the upper third.
  • •Avoid excessive crown height if balance is the goal.
Run the hairstyle finder →

Glasses

  • •Taller lenses can add vertical coverage and visual width.
  • •A pronounced brow line can break up facial length.
  • •Avoid very shallow frames if proportional balance is the goal.
Run the glasses finder →

Beard shapes

  • •Keeping the beard shorter at the chin and fuller at the cheeks adds width instead of length.
  • •A long, pointed beard extends the outline further, which works against balance if that is the goal.
  • •A moustache introduces a horizontal line across the middle of the face.

Contour and makeup

  • •Contour along the hairline and under the chin visually shortens the vertical run.
  • •Blush placed horizontally across the cheeks rather than angled upward adds width.
  • •A flatter, more horizontal brow shape counters the vertical emphasis.

Earrings, necklines and hats

  • •Wide or clustered earrings add horizontal width; long drops extend the length.
  • •Boat and wide necklines broaden the line below the face.
  • •Tall lenses and a strong brow bar on frames break up the vertical run; wide-brimmed hats add width.

About the oblong shape

Measure your own face free →
Is an oblong face the same as a rectangular face?+

The terms are used interchangeably in most styling guides. Some sources reserve rectangular for an oblong face that also has a squared jaw corner; this site treats them as one profile and reports the jaw angle separately.

How long does a face have to be to count as oblong?+

This detector places the oblong profile at a length-to-cheek-width ratio of about 1.64, against roughly 1.44 for oval. There is no hard cutoff — the detector reports how close you are to each, which is why the result is a distribution rather than a single label.
